title: Ways to judge progress
summary: Weight trend, body fat, tape, strength or the Fitness score: what each tells you and when it misleads.
text: progress has more than one measure, and each one answers a different question. this page sets out what each measure tells you, what it cannot tell you, and which one to trust when they seem to disagree. progress. when to use it the scale moved but you do not know whether to believe it. you wonder what body fat, tape and strength each have to do with the number on progress. you want to know why the fitness score moved little after a good week. the measures weight trend: the 7-day average your weight can move up and down by a kilo or so in a day because of water, food and salt. one weigh-in tells you very little. forma shows your weigh-ins as dots and the average of the last 7 days as a line. the average shows the real direction; single weigh-ins are for the record. the average also drives your verdict at the top of progress. it compares your pace per week with the aim for your goal: -0.75 to -0.50 percent of bodyweight a week on a cut, -0.25 to +0.25 maintaining, and +0.25 to +0.50 on a bulk. a loss faster than the "too fast" line is where muscle starts to go. the average needs weigh-ins to work. a week with none means no current average; one new weigh-in restarts it. you do not need a reading every day. body fat the body row on progress holds your body fat and lean mass: readings from apple health, clinic scans you add, and an estimate from your tape. a scale or a clinic scan is preferred. the tape estimate is only a second opinion. your goal (eat up, hold or cut) is decided from this number against a range that depends on your sex: women under 18 percent eat up, 18 to 23 hold, over 23 cut; men under 10 eat up, 10 to 15 hold, over 15 cut. tap why this goal on that screen to see your own range and the working. it misleads when devices change. different devices read differently, so keep using the same one, and read the direction over several weeks rather than the exact level. tape measurements a full tape is all six sites (waist, neck, chest, upper arm, thigh, hips) in one sitting, once a month. waist and neck also give the body-fat estimate that sits next to your other readings. if you skip a site, the entry is kept, but it does not reset the monthly clock. the tape misleads when you compare one month with the next too closely. an arm does not grow much in 28 days; several months of tape is the real signal. strength history & reports shows sets per muscle for your week; around 10 to 20 sets a week for each muscle is the range most people build in. each lift is shown as an estimated one-rep max from your best set each day. the estimate misleads if you read it as a real maximum. it is a trend line: only the direction matters, and the same lift over time is what to compare. the fitness score the fitness score gives each area a score out of 10 and one number across them. it is slow on purpose: every area looks at the last 28 days, and one snapshot is saved a week. sleep and protein need at least 7 nights or 7 logged days before they count. a body-fat reading older than 120 days stops counting and shows as out of date. when you are cutting, keeping your lifts about where they were (down no more than 2 percent) still scores good or better for strength. a worked example sam (88 kg, on a cut) weighs in each morning. two weeks of weigh-ins look like this (each average is the mean of the readings from the last 7 days, including that day): date weigh-in (kg) 7-day average (kg) 26 oct 88.4 88.40 1 nov 87.9 88.31 4 nov 87.5 88.04 8 nov 87.1 87.60 single weigh-ins jump around by half a kilo or more (88.9 then 88.1 on back-to-back mornings), while the average moves smoothly. on 8 nov the average is 87.60; a week earlier (1 nov) it was 88.31. that is a change of -0.71 kg, or -0.81 percent of bodyweight per week. the cut band is -0.75 to -0.50, so the verdict class is "faster than aim": the loss is a little quicker than planned. forma keeps "too fast" as a separate verdict, and a loss past that line is where muscle starts to go. good to know limit: the fitness score is a summary of your own numbers, and the body-fat rule that sets your goal is forma's own rule of thumb. tip: touch a chart and slide your finger along it to read the exact value for any day. note: weigh at a similar time, for example after the toilet and before breakfast, and several times a week, so the average has something to work with. related weight and the 7-day average body fat and lean mass tape measurements the fitness score

title: Ways to log training
summary: Live in the gym, import history, or fill in afterwards.
text: forma records a session in three ways: log it set by set while you lift, import the history from the app you are switching from, or add a missed session afterwards. all three become normal sessions in one history, and the coach plans from that history. when to use it you have your phone with you on the gym floor and a few seconds between sets. you are switching from another app and have months of workouts worth keeping. the phone stayed in the locker, or you lost track of the session, and you still want the day on record. your old app can export a csv, and you would rather not start your numbers from zero. logging live in the gym logging works with no signal. on train, tap start. it carries the session's name, for example start push. your lifts are listed with their sets and reps. tap a lift to open it. the weight and reps are filled in from last time or from the plan. change anything that was different. tap log set 1, then log set 2, and so on. forma asks one question: how many more could you have done? tap 0, 1-2 or 3+. tap skip if you would rather not say. the rest timer starts. when it ends, tap the next set and log it. tap another set if you did one more than planned. when the last set is logged, you go back to the list of lifts. warm-up sets are marked w1, w2 and never count as volume, recovery or records. tip: it costs one tap to answer "how many more could you have done?" that answer lets the next session push a little harder or hold back. answer it when you can. importing your history most training apps can export your history as a csv file. forma reads that file on your phone, matches your exercises to its own lifts, and adds the workouts to history. nothing is uploaded. in your other app, look for export data, export workouts or download my data. it is usually in settings or profile. choose csv if it asks for a format, and save the file to files or icloud drive, or share it to this phone. open settings, then import workout history. on an empty train screen, you can get there under import workouts instead. tap choose a file and pick the csv. check the preview: how many workouts and sets, the date range, and the weight unit. if the file does not say kilograms or pounds, forma asks once. for each exercise forma could not place, make the choice: match it to one of forma's lifts, keep it as its own lift, or skip it. forma remembers your answers for next time. tap import. when it finishes, tap done to see the workouts in history. note: importing the same file twice adds nothing; sets forma already has are left out. changed your mind later? tap undo this import on the result page. it removes exactly what that import added, and nothing else. tip: no file to import? on the same screen, tap enter my main lifts. one last weight and reps per lift is enough for a sensible first week. filling in afterwards forgot to log, or could not use the phone that day? a missed session can still go on record. tap the clock button at the top right of train to open history & reports. open history and tap the plus button (add a missed session). pick the day: today or any of the last three weeks. choose a lift, enter the sets you remember, and save. it shows in that day's session without a duration. you can also correct existing sessions. open one in history, tap a set, and change its weight or reps, or tap delete set. deleting a session asks first and cannot be undone. good to know imported sessions are marked as imported. they set your starting weights and recovery. your own logged sessions count for more as you add them. imported workouts are normal workouts. you can correct a set or delete a session in history, like one you logged yourself. the import leaves out cardio rows with no reps. set notes in the file are not kept; the sets themselves are. changing past sets changes your recovery readings, your next weights and your insights, so they follow what you really did. related today's session log your sets bring your workout history past sessions and reports

title: A beginner's week
summary: An invented week with the numbers Forma works out.
text: one invented person, one ordinary week, and the targets forma works out day by day. read it to see what a normal week of numbers looks like before you log anything yourself. when to use it you are new and want to know what to expect from your first weeks. you wonder why the target is higher on a training day than on a rest day. you want to see where the protein, carbs and fat in your target come from. how forma builds a day's target forma builds each day the same way, from the numbers you have already given it: it starts with your resting burn, worked out from your weight, height, age and sex (the mifflin-st jeor formula). when forma already has a body-composition reading, it works the same figure from your lean mass instead. it adds everyday movement: 10 percent of the resting burn. on a training day it adds the exercise the day should bring: about 250 kcal for a strength day until forma has at least three of your own sessions to learn from. a rest day adds nothing. your goal then moves the day. on maintain, it stays where it is. it splits the calories: protein is a fixed amount per kilogram of bodyweight, fat is 27.5 percent of the calories, and carbs fill what is left. a worked example amira is a woman, 62 kg, 165 cm, 34 years old. her goal is maintain, and she trains 3 strength days a week. her resting burn is 1,320 kcal. her week, as forma sets it: day kind calories protein carbs fat monday strength 1,702 kcal 112 g 197 g 52 g tuesday rest 1,452 kcal 112 g 152 g 44 g wednesday strength 1,702 kcal 112 g 197 g 52 g thursday rest 1,452 kcal 112 g 152 g 44 g friday strength 1,702 kcal 112 g 197 g 52 g saturday rest 1,452 kcal 112 g 152 g 44 g sunday rest 1,452 kcal 112 g 152 g 44 g for a strength day, forma's own wording is: "strength day: 1,702 kcal — rest days are 1,452." how to read it: protein never moves between rest and training days; the extra 250 kcal on a strength day all go to carbs and fat. three training days spread across the week make an average of 1,559 kcal a day. that is what her body is expected to use on an ordinary day of the week. good to know the 250 kcal on a strength day is an estimate until forma has three of your own sessions. after that, forma uses the median burn from your own recent sessions; on a day your watch has measured the training, the measured figure is used instead of the estimate. protein is set per kilogram of bodyweight. on maintain it is 1.8 g/kg, which for amira's 62 kg gives the 112 g she sees every day. the target is never lower than the higher of your resting burn and a common least-to-eat guideline. amira's target comes nowhere near the floor. some people's do; forma holds the target up and says when it does. you never type a calorie number. forma works the target out; the goal is what you change. these targets are information and estimates from your own entries, not medical advice. talk to a doctor before you change how you eat. related your day target, and why it moves a cutting week a gaining week ways to judge progress

title: A cutting week
summary: Losing fat while keeping protein high.
text: a cut is a fixed deficit on your ordinary eating, with protein held high. this page shows one invented week, so you can see where the numbers land before you start one. when to use it you are about to start cutting and want to see what a week of targets looks like. you wonder why your rest and training days are closer together than you expected. you want to check what a day of a cut gives you in protein, carbs and fat. how a cutting day is built a cutting day is built like any other day, with two differences: the goal offset and the protein figure. resting burn: worked out from weight, height, age and sex (the mifflin-st jeor formula). when forma already has a body-composition reading, it works the same figure from your lean mass instead. everyday movement is added: 10 percent of the resting burn. a training day adds its exercise: about 250 kcal for a strength day until forma has at least three of your own sessions to learn from. the cut is applied: about 17.5 percent fewer calories than the average day of your week uses. that is a fixed deficit, and it lands on every day. a check against the floor: the target never goes below the higher of your resting burn and the common least-to-eat guideline for your sex. when the floor holds the target up, forma says so. protein is set per kilogram of bodyweight (2.1 g/kg on a cut), fat is 27.5 percent of the calories, and carbs fill what is left. a worked example sam is a man, 88 kg, 180 cm, 38 years old. his goal is cut, and he trains 4 strength days a week. his resting burn is 1,820 kcal, and his average training week would use about 2,145 kcal a day. the cut takes 375 kcal off that average day. his week, as forma sets it: day kind calories protein carbs fat monday strength 1,877 kcal 185 g 156 g 57 g tuesday strength 1,877 kcal 185 g 156 g 57 g wednesday rest 1,820 kcal 185 g 144 g 56 g thursday strength 1,877 kcal 185 g 156 g 57 g friday strength 1,877 kcal 185 g 156 g 57 g saturday rest 1,820 kcal 185 g 144 g 56 g sunday rest 1,820 kcal 185 g 144 g 56 g how to read it: his protein never moves; only carbs and fat do. his rest days sit at exactly his resting burn of 1,820 kcal, because the floor holds the target up. the unrestricted number would be lower, and forma says when it does this. a strength day is only a little above it, so rest and training days sit close together on a cut this deep. protein is where the 2.1 g/kg on a cut shows: for sam's 88 kg that is 185 g a day, and the fat at 27.5 percent of the calories is about 56 to 57 g. what remains of each day's calories is carbs. good to know protein on a cut is a floor, not a budget: going over is good. calories, carbs and fat are budgets, and calories are the one to watch. the target follows your 7-day average weight, not a single weigh-in. weigh in a few times a week; the average is what counts. the scale confirms the pace over weeks, not days. what you lose is what the scale shows, not what the plan predicted. you never type a calorie number. forma works the target out; the goal is what you change. this page is information and estimates, not medical or diet advice. talk to a doctor or dietitian before eating at a deficit, especially if you have a medical condition. related your day target, and why it moves a beginner's week a gaining week weight and the 7-day average

title: A gaining week
summary: Eating for muscle with a small surplus.
text: a gaining week is a week in which you eat a little more than you burn, so your training has something to build from. this page explains how forma sets the numbers, what a week looks like, and what to expect on training days versus rest days. forma does not ask you for a calorie number. it works the target out from your body, your movement and your goal. on a gain (the goal forma labels eat up), a small surplus is added on top of what your body is expected to use. the surplus is deliberate: the aim is a slow gain that mostly goes to muscle, not a fast one. when to use it you train to add muscle and you are at a body-fat level where gaining is the sensible direction. forma decides a goal from your measured body fat; until you have a reading, you choose the goal yourself in settings under goal. your 7-day average weight has been flat for weeks while you train hard, and you want it to start moving up slowly. you want different targets for rest days and training days, instead of one flat number that is wrong half the week. note: forma gives information and estimates, not medical advice. for anything medical, ask a doctor. step by step weigh in a few times during the week: tap add weigh-in on today, or let apple health bring the readings in. open settings and check height, birth date and sex. a wrong entry shifts every number. under goal, choose eat up. forma may have chosen it for you already if your body fat is measured. open fuel and read today's target on the ring. on a day with a strength session it is higher; on rest days, lower. log your meals with the plus button (add food) and land near the target for the day you are on. a worked example lee is an invented trainee. his data: a man, 68 kg, 178 cm tall, age 22, with 4 strength days a week and the bulk goal. forma estimates the resting burn from weight, height, age and sex. then it adds everyday movement (10 percent of the resting burn), expected exercise (about 250 kcal on a strength day until it has learned from your own sessions), and the bulk surplus (+250 kcal, which is 12.5 percent of his average-day maintenance). resting burn average-day maintenance goal offset rest day target strength day target lee 1,688 kcal 2,000 kcal +250 kcal 2,107 kcal 2,357 kcal the full targets, with macros: lee (bulk) calories protein carbs fat rest day 2,107 kcal 116 g 267 g 64 g strength day 2,357 kcal 116 g 311 g 72 g how to read it: the surplus only needs to average out over the week. eating near 2,107 on rest days and 2,357 on strength days lands him on the intended pace, about 250 kcal up per day on average. protein stays at 116 g on both kinds of day, because it is fixed per kilogram of bodyweight (1.7 g/kg on a bulk). the extra 250 kcal on a strength day goes almost entirely into carbs (267 g to 311 g), with a couple of grams more fat. for his weekly total, that is roughly 15,700 kcal: four strength days and three rest days at those targets. forma checks the 7-day average weight each week to see whether the pace is working. good to know the coach acts on your 7-day average weight, not a single weigh-in. if your body fat is measured, forma may set the goal for you: for men, it chooses eat up when the reading is below about 10 percent. the surplus is small on purpose: a bulk adds about 12.5 percent to average-day maintenance. there is no calorie field to fill in: forma works the number out for you. protein does not move between rest and training days. only carbs and fat do, because training changes the energy you use, not how much protein you need to keep muscle. protein is a floor, not a budget: going over it is good. calories, carbs and fat are budgets; going over them is what to avoid. carbs are the flexible macro. they take whatever calories are left after protein and fat. the grams are estimates; being reasonably close matters more than hitting the exact number. forma never suggests less than your resting burn, or a common least-to-eat guideline for your sex (1,500 kcal for men, 1,200 for women). on a bulk this floor is unlikely to matter. the scale confirms the pace over weeks, not days. a kilo of change in a day is water and food, not progress lost. prefer one number for every day? the diet coach offers that when it works alone: a flat everyday target with no training-day split. limit: these targets are estimates from the numbers you enter. if
